## The question one level up

Almost every agent benchmark asks the same question: *how good is this agent — or
this base model — at task τ?* You fix a task suite, you swap in agents or models,
and you read off a leaderboard.

MAArena asks a different question, one level up:

> **Given a fixed seed agent and a fixed budget, can a _method_ improve that
> agent's held-out pass rate — and is the gain worth what it cost?**

The unit of evaluation is not the agent and not the base model. It is the
**meta-optimizer**: the procedure that takes an agent and tries to make it better —
by editing its prompts, rewriting its code, evolving its workflow, or letting it
rewrite itself. GEPA, AFlow, AdaEvolve, Meta-Harness, a raw coding-agent session,
a self-improving Gödel-machine-style loop: these are the things under test. The
agent they operate on is held fixed so that **the method is the only variable.**

This reframing is the whole point. There is a fast-growing literature of
"self-improving," "agent-optimizing," and "meta-agent" methods, each reporting
gains on its own agent, its own task, its own budget. Those numbers are not
comparable. MAArena fixes the agent, the task carrier, the budget, and the scoring
so that a claim like *"method M lifts this agent by Δ at this cost"* means the same
thing across methods.

## The headline number: Δ-over-seed, cost-regularized

Every run reports a **Δ-over-seed** — the improvement the method achieves over the
agent it started from, measured on a sealed test split:

$$
\text{score}(\text{method}) \;=\; \text{test\_pass\_rate}\big(\text{method.best()}\big)
\;-\; \text{test\_pass\_rate}(\text{seed}).
$$

The seed agent's own sealed-test pass rate is the **null baseline** — the floor
that does nothing. This has two immediate consequences:

- **The seed is the floor.** We report the *lift*, not the absolute pass rate. A
  benchmark cell where the untouched seed already wins is a bad cell — the method
  had no room to help.
- **The gain is never reported alone.** It is always paired with what it consumed.
  The headline artifact is not a scalar but an **anytime curve**: best-so-far
  sealed-test score plotted against ledger spend (dollars, tokens, rollouts,
  wall-clock). A method that buys two points of accuracy for \$0.80 and a method
  that buys three points for \$150 are telling very different stories, and the
  curve shows both.

Cost-regularization is a first-class design principle, not a footnote. Sample
efficiency — how much data and money a method needs to climb — is a scored axis.

## How a run is specified

A single run is a point in a small, explicit configuration space:

```
   run  =  ( BENCHMARK ,  SEED ,  METHOD ,  BUDGET + RNG )
            the carrier    the worker   the         resource
            + its harness   optimized    optimizer   envelope
```

| Axis | What it varies |
|---|---|
| **Benchmark** | the carrier task suite and its harness / modality |
| **Seed** | the worker agent (a launchable `agent/` tree) being optimized |
| **Method** | the meta-optimizer under test |
| **Budget + seed** | the ledger cap and the RNG seed |

Because the *same* method runs across benchmarks and seeds, a result is never a
single conflated number. It is always "method M lifts *this seed* on *this carrier*
by Δ at *this cost*." The rest of this post walks each axis, then the protocol that
binds them.

## The carriers: four benchmarks

The task suites are the ground the methods stand on. Each ships its data and is
scored by a trusted, benchmark-owned harness.

| Benchmark | Modality | Scoring |
|---|---|---|
| **gpqa** | one-shot graduate-level science multiple-choice QA | exact-choice: the worker emits a final `(X)` option letter |
| **charxiv** | multimodal chart QA (chart image + question) | a faithful-reasoning judge over the worker's `Answer:` line |
| **tau2** | interactive tool-use with a simulated user (customer-service dialog) | the τ²-bench task verifier over the full dialog |
| **tb2** | launchable terminal / sysadmin / coding tasks in Docker | a task verifier that runs *inside* the container |

These four span a deliberate spectrum:

- **gpqa** and **charxiv** are the **one-shot form** — the runner feeds an instance
  and reads an answer. charxiv is the suite's multimodal member (a vision-capable
  worker reads the chart).
- **tau2** and **tb2** are the **launchable-agent form** — the worker is a program
  the runner launches against a disposable environment (a simulated dialog, a
  Harbor/Docker container) over a fixed action channel. Here the environment and
  the verifier are benchmark-owned and trusted, and the *worker itself* makes
  metered LLM calls, tracked separately from the method's own calls.

Every benchmark shares **one** metered runner, **one** ledger, and **one** sealed
test, which is what makes cost comparisons hold *across* benchmarks and not just
within one.

## The workers: five seeds per benchmark

For each benchmark, MAArena ships **five seed agents** — one base plus four
literature-pattern variants — each a launchable `agent/` tree that satisfies the
benchmark's I/O contract.

| Benchmark | base seed | variant seeds |
|---|---|---|
| **gpqa** | `gpqa` (chain-of-thought) | Program-of-Thoughts · multi-agent debate · self-refine · Tree-of-Thoughts |
| **tau2** | `tau2` (ReAct) | plan-then-act · ReWOO · reflect/self-correct · scratchpad memory |
| **charxiv** | `charxiv` (direct/CoT VLM) | PoT-over-table · crop-zoom re-query · draft→verify→revise · K-sample self-consistency |

The seed roster is the **abstraction axis** of the experiment: each variant is a
minimal, faithful abstraction of a technique from the agent literature, and each
exposes a *different* edit surface. A method's lift therefore has to generalize
across agent *shapes*, not just squeeze one hand-picked pipeline. Each seed also
ships a small multi-rep baseline pass rate — the floor its Δ is measured against.

## The optimizers: the roster, on a coupling × surface grid

The methods are the actual subject of the benchmark. The current roster:

| Method | What it is |
|---|---|
| **GEPA** | reflective genetic-Pareto prompt search over the declared prompt surface [@gepa] |
| **AFlow** | MCTS search over agentic workflows-as-code (graph + prompts) [@aflow] |
| **AdaEvolve** | adaptive multi-island evolutionary program search with a pluggable fitness [@adaevolve] |
| **Meta-Harness** (`mh_paper`) | a coding-agent proposer with unrestricted access to the full search history — prior source, scores, raw traces — Pareto-selected [@mh] |
| **coding_agent** | the unstructured coding-agent baseline: one long-lived session editing the agent in place, self-stopping on plateau or budget |
| **HGM** | endogenous / self-improving: the agent proposes its own successor via its own `self_improve.py` |
| **prompt_hill** | a walking-skeleton method that hill-climbs the system prompt via failure-driven edits |

To make sense of a roster this heterogeneous, MAArena classifies each method on two
independent axes.

**Surface — what medium the method edits:**

- *prompt surface*: the seed's tunable text, declared in `agent/PROMPTS.json`.
  Prompt-optimizers share one declared surface per benchmark, which is what makes
  their comparison fair.
- *whole-program*: the entire `agent/` tree — pipeline code, control flow, workflow
  graph, and parameters.

**Coupling — how bound the optimizer is to the agent it optimizes:**

- *agnostic / seed-transforming*: takes an arbitrary seed and returns an improved
  agent of the same kind. Directly comparable on a shared seed.
- *agent-native, exogenous*: the optimizer owns the agent's *representation* (a
  workflow graph, a program archive) and is anchored to its own genesis; the output
  is the method's own artifact, not the seed transformed.
- *agent-native, endogenous*: the optimizer **is** the worker — it rewrites its own
  source.

Populated with the roster:

| coupling ╲ surface | **prompt** | **whole-program** |
|---|---|---|
| **agnostic / seed-transforming** | GEPA · prompt_hill | Meta-Harness · coding_agent |
| **agent-native · exogenous** | — | AFlow · AdaEvolve |
| **agent-native · endogenous** | — | HGM |

Coupling is the load-bearing distinction: *does the method's output stay in the
seed's representation, or move into the method's own?* Seed-transforming methods
run on the shared seed grid and are compared head-to-head on Δ-over-seed.
Agent-native methods carry their own genesis, so they are still scored by
Δ-over-seed on the shared dataset at a cost, but they do not sweep a foreign seed
grid — comparing them to prompt-tuners on "who edits the same prompt best" would be
a category error.

## The protocol: freedom inside, discipline at the boundary

Here is the design decision that makes the rest work. A meta-optimizer is a wildly
varied thing — a Python search loop, a coding-agent session, a shell pipeline, a
self-modifying program. If the benchmark forced all of them through a rigid
`optimize()` API with a mandated candidate format and a fixed feedback string, two
things would break: faithful re-hosting of published methods, and the freedom those
methods need to do what they actually do.

So MAArena inverts the usual contract. **The method is free inside its workspace;
the discipline lives entirely at the boundary.**

### The workspace

Each run gets a workspace and is otherwise unconstrained:

```
workspace/
  agent/      # THE worker to improve — the method maintains its current best here,
              # in place. This exact directory faces the sealed test at run end.
  versions/   # framework-written archive of every registered version (one per subdir)
  train/      # the train split, as the dataset ships it
  logs/       # rollout results from the method's train calls land here
  ...         # anything else the method wants: scratch, archives, its own tools
```

There is **no `build()`**, no mandated candidate format, no fixed event
vocabulary, and no separate submission directory. The submission *is* `agent/`, in
place. Versions enter the version graph (a `commons-vcs` store) through three
triggers — an evaluation observing the directory, a voluntary `register` hook, or a
`stamp` checkpoint — never on raw file writes.

### The trusted runner: three endpoints, one disclosure ladder

All the discipline is concentrated in a single trusted, host-side runner service
that owns Docker, the graders, and the held-out splits. It exposes three
budget-metered endpoints at three levels of disclosure, plus a free meter read:

| Endpoint | Returns | Disclosure |
|---|---|---|
| `run_train(agent, task_ids, trajectory=k)` | per-task observations **including the gold** | **full** |
| `score_dev(agent, n?, reps?)` | one scalar, nothing else | **scalar-only** |
| `score_test(agent)` | framework-invoked only; never returned to the method | **sealed** |
| `spend()` | read-only view of the method's own meter | free |

This is the **disclosure ladder**, and its integrity is *physical, not
contractual*. Held-out data never crosses the boundary, so there is nothing for a
method to leak: dev returns a bare float; test is never returned at all. There is
no "strict mode" a method must promise to honor — the channel simply does not
carry per-instance dev or test data. Test is scored by the framework, on the
method's stamped checkpoints, after the run.

### What a method actually observes

When a method calls `run_train`, each per-task record carries **two independent
facets**:

1. **The dataset verdict** (owned by the grader): the task input, the worker's
   answer, a `passed`/`score`/`exit_status` core, and a *structured* `detail`
   verdict with a `kind` discriminator (`qa`, `dialog`, `terminal`) so a method
   reads the keys it understands. Grading is always terminal, never per-turn.
2. **The worker trajectory** (owned by the log): the last *k* turns reconstructed
   into a **uniform** shape — the same on every benchmark —
   `{turn_idx, actor, message, reasoning, actions, observations, error}`, plus a
   grep-able path to the full raw trace.

The split matters because a harness is a *(dataset × worker-agent)* pairing: the
verdict's shape is dataset-determined, the trajectory's shape is
I/O-contract-determined. Because the verdict is self-describing and the trajectory
is uniform, a method needs *one* generic renderer, not one per dataset. Different
methods consume different facets — Meta-Harness greps raw traces, GEPA folds a few
reconstructed turns into its reflection step, a coding-agent may ignore both and
build its own instruments from the raw `train/` data. *Which* signal a method reads
is itself a research observable we record.

## The comparison spine: one ledger, one sealed score

Cross-method comparison rests on exactly three things: **worker versions × ledger
spend × official sealed scores**. Nothing else.

The **ledger** is the meta-economy record. It folds in real time — advancing on
every LLM call and every rollout, never in post-hoc batches — and attributes spend
*per actor*: the method's own calls (`meta`) are tracked separately from the calls
the worker agent makes while being evaluated (`worker`). It tracks per-actor tokens
(in/out/cache), dollars (provider-reported where available), rollouts, endpoint
calls by type, and wall-clock. Crucially, **dev checks are metered against the
method's budget** — checking held-out performance is a strategic spend, which both
reflects reality and economically bounds the "hammer dev until it climbs"
degeneracy.

The **anytime curve** is built from `stamp` checkpoints. A `stamp` freezes the
ledger reading and registers the current `agent/` in the version graph; those
checkpoints are what the framework hidden-tests post-hoc. The plotted curve is
therefore *(spend-at-stamp × sealed-test score)*, best-so-far. A method that never
stamps still gets an automatic run-end "final" stamp, so every run yields at least
one curve point. The best-by-dev version is kept as a free *diagnostic* (the gap
between final and argmax-dev tells you about selection quality) but is never the
official number.

A deliberate consequence of "standardize outcomes, not processes": **method
interiors are never compared as metrics.** One method emitting rich Pareto-frontier
events and another emitting nothing is a difference in *color*, not a difference in
*score*. Comparing on interior richness would just reward whoever instrumented more
— so the ledger spine, and only the ledger spine, carries the comparison.

## Two commitments that protect validity

**Faithfulness.** The vendored optimizers run through their own sanctioned seams
with zero source edits — a run with no overrides reproduces the published method.
Methods select candidates with their *native* mechanism; `dev` is an *optional*
scalar check, not a mandated selection gate, and only `test` is ever sealed. The
goal is that MAArena measures the method as its authors built it, not a
benchmark-flavored reinterpretation of it.

**Isolation.** The method process runs jailed, with its workspace as the sole
writable root, because it executes LLM-authored code against a harness that owns
the answer key — for a benchmark, sandbox escape is a *validity* problem
(reward-hacking the scorer), not only a safety one. Where the jail cannot be
applied, the downgrade is recorded loudly and visibly, so it can never masquerade
as a clean run. (Docker-based benchmarks are a known containment gap, tracked
openly and excluded from adversarial runs until closed.)

## Why these choices, together

Step back and the pieces form one argument:

1. **Cost-regularized** — a gain is nothing without its price, so the anytime curve,
   not a scalar, is the deliverable.
2. **Sample efficiency is first-class** — every rollout, dev checks included, is
   metered, so data appetite is scored.
3. **Faithful methods** — vendored engines run through native seams with native
   selection, so we measure the real method.
4. **The seed is the floor** — the headline is Δ-over-seed, not absolute accuracy.
5. **Reproducibility via multi-seed + CI** — agent rollouts are nondeterministic
   (the executor rejects `temperature=0` and can flip pass↔fail on re-run), so the
   intended reading is always multi-seed with confidence intervals, never a single
   number.
6. **One shared contract** — one metered runner, one ledger, one sealed test, so
   cross-benchmark cost comparison actually holds.

Freedom inside the workspace lets any method be itself; discipline at the boundary —
the disclosure ladder, the per-actor ledger, the sealed test — is what makes their
results mean the same thing.

## What's next

That is the *setup*: the question, the axes, the carriers, the seeds, the roster,
and the protocol that scores them all on one spine. The **second post** turns to the
*findings* — what happens when you actually run this grid: which methods lift which
agents, where the money goes, how badly dev overfits test, and what the anytime
curves reveal that a leaderboard hides.
